name: consumer-driven-contract-test
intent: Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment.
problem: Independently released consumers and providers must keep working together, yet the only reliable check is a shared end-to-end environment per pair - slow, brittle and usually out of date; at the same time the provider cannot see which parts of its API each consumer actually exercises, so every refactoring is a guess about who will break.
context: HTTP/request-reply, messaging and gRPC integrations where consumer and provider are owned by different teams on different release cadences and each consumer uses only a narrow slice of the provider's surface. It assumes the provider team is willing to run verification of consumer contracts in its own build; without that half, the consumer test is only a better mock.
benefits: Runs at unit-test speed: compatibility is checked without deploying either side, so integration mistakes surface in the consumer's or the provider's build instead of in a shared environment.
Only the interactions consumers actually use are pinned, so the rest of the provider stays free to change - that is what turns independent deployability from aspiration into practice.
The contract is a by-product of tests the consumer team would write anyway, and it doubles as executable documentation of how the API is really used.
Failures are attributed: verification names the consumer, the interaction and the mismatching field, which collapses the debugging time typical of an end-to-end failure.
Language- and protocol-neutral carrier: the same contract format is verified by any implementation in any language, for HTTP, messages and gRPC.
Gives deployment decisions evidence: verified compatibility per consumer/provider version can gate a release instead of relying on whether the shared test environment happened to be current.
tradeoffs: Only the exercised interactions are covered; a consumer path that no test touched can still be broken by a provider change without any contract failing.
Loose matchers buy stability at the price of precision: a type matcher accepts any string, so semantic changes (relative instead of absolute URLs, changed units) pass verification.

Provider states are a second, hand-maintained contract: each state must set up provider data, and a state that drifts from the interaction's assumptions produces failures that look like provider bugs.
The guarantee exists only if the provider actually runs verification and gates deployment on it; where verification is skipped, ignored, or allowed to fail, the contract degrades into documentation.

Every consumer adds interactions to the union the provider must honour, so a popular provider accumulates a de-facto compatibility surface that resists cleanup - removing an old consumer's interaction becomes a negotiation.
Extra moving parts on both sides: mock servers, a contract broker and publishing/verification pipelines, plus per-test mock servers that interact badly with HTTP connection pooling.
Interactions are verified in isolation, so sequences cannot be chained (write then read) and a misnamed field can be accepted silently by the provider - the classic garbage-in, garbage-out trap.

participants.responsibility: The client code that issues the requests or consumes the messages; it is the code under test and the only legitimate source of the contract.
Drives the real client against the mock provider, asserts how the client handles the response, and produces the contract as a side-effect of passing.
Serves the declared responses and validates the client's actual requests against the declared expectations; any unmatched or missing request fails the test.
Machine-readable record of the required interactions - request, response, matching rules and the provider state each interaction needs.
Replays every interaction of the contract against the real provider and reports mismatches per consumer and interaction.
Establishes the fixture conditions a contract declares (data, feature flags, authentication) before the interaction is replayed, in isolation.
Stores contracts together with verification results, tells each side which versions are compatible, and answers the deployability question.

use_cases: Microservice landscapes where a front end, a mobile app or another service consumes an API released by a different team on its own schedule.
A provider team that must refactor or replace internals and needs to know, before merging, which consumer expectations it is about to break.
Mobile or desktop clients that cannot be deployed in lockstep with the backend, so each client's expectations must hold against every backend version.

Event- and message-based integrations (Kafka, SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ) where the consumer processes messages produced by another team; contracts pin the message body shape and metadata (topic, headers, content-type) while abstracting the transport.
Migration or strangler-fig work, where a replacement provider must be proven compatible with the existing consumers before traffic is moved.
Using the contract as the source of stubs for development and integration environments, so those environments no longer need the real provider.

BFF (Backend for Frontend) patterns where each frontend channel (web, mobile, third-party) has its own contract with a shared backend, allowing independent evolution of each BFF without cross-channel breakage.

Multi-team Kafka event streaming where consumers (downstream services) define which topics, partitions and message schemas they depend on, so producers can evolve events without silently breaking subscribers; Pact message pacts handle both JSON and Schema Registry messages (with magic bytes for Avro/Protobuf over Schema Registry).

gRPC service integrations where protocol buffer message shapes are exercised by the actual consumer client code, pinning the wire format, service method signatures and metadata the consumer actually calls; synchronous message pacts cover the request-response pairing.

Breaking up a monolith: individual microservices are extracted and their CDC contracts verify that the new service boundaries behave identically to the original module interfaces before traffic is migrated.
Schema Registry integrations (Confluent, AWS Glue) where consumers pin compatible message schemas and producers must not publish breaking schemas without migrating all dependent consumers first.

Third-party or vendor API integrations where the consumer team cannot rely on the provider to run verification: the consumer-side mock-only workflow with published contracts documents expectations even without provider participation.

Webhook and callback integrations where a provider calls a consumer-defined endpoint; CDC captures the consumer's expected payload shape, headers and authentication, and the provider verifies it can deliver to that shape.

Contract migration at scale: when a provider must migrate from v1 to v2 of an API, CDC with pending/wip pacts allows the provider to signal new expectations to consumers without blocking either side's pipeline while migration is in progress.

Spring Cloud Contract in JVM/Spring landscapes: the consumer's contract change lands in the producer's repository (or an external contract repo), the producer build generates verification tests from the contract DSL, and the consumer develops against StubRunner-served WireMock stubs pulled from an artifact repository (Nexus/Artifactory) - the contract is the single artifact both sides build from.

Nubank replaced its flaky shared-environment end-to-end suite with consumer-driven contract tests to regain deploy velocity - the public account of the pattern paying off as an e2e-substitute at a single organisation rather than as an addition to it.

Large polyglot estates such as JSTOR/ITHAKA (300+ microservices, 12+ teams, Pact) and M1 Finance (Pact plus PactFlow rolled out to 17 teams in under six months): the broker's compatibility matrix replaces per-pair end-to-end environments as the release gate.
avoid_when: Consumer and provider live in one repository and are always deployed together: ordinary integration or component tests cover the boundary with far less machinery.
The provider cannot be made to run verification (third-party or closed-source API): only the mock half is possible, so recorded fixtures or a stub server is the honest choice.
The goal is to test consumer behaviour, UI flows or provider business logic: contract tests pin the shape of the interaction, not the semantics either side computes.
A stable, provider-owned schema already protects the boundary (published OpenAPI/protobuf with provider-side breaking-change detection) and no consumer-specific obligations exist.
The contract is wanted only as a stub for local development: generate that stub from a shared schema or fixtures instead of standing up publishing and verification pipelines on both sides.

The domain requires semantic or behavioural correctness verification: contract tests verify wire-format compatibility in isolation and cannot verify computed values, conditional logic, side-effects, or end-to-end data flows.

Teams are unwilling to treat the broker as production infrastructure: without broker uptime, publishing and verification are blocked; if the team cannot commit to running the broker reliably, the contract pipeline will silently degrade.
anti_patterns: Using the mock provider as a stub: responses are declared but the request the client actually sent is never asserted, so the contract records nothing about the consumer's expectations.

Contract tests written as functional tests of the provider - asserting business rules, data volumes or formatting the consumer never reads - which makes the contract brittle and the provider's legitimate changes fail.
Hand-written or provider-authored contracts published as if the consumers had produced them: the provider ends up verifying its own assumptions while real consumer usage stays invisible.

Scope creep upward: driving the contract through UI or whole-application tests multiplies interactions and produces a cartesian explosion of verification work with almost no added compatibility coverage.
Treating contract verification as a replacement for end-to-end or functional testing, then discovering the gaps in production.
Letting verification results rot: contracts published but never verified, or verification failures tolerated as 'known', so the contract keeps a green badge while the integration is already broken.
Treating the broker as a passive store: publishing contracts without wiring can-i-deploy checks into the deployment pipeline means compatibility is tracked but never enforced.
Over-specifying provider states: each interaction declares an elaborate state setup that is expensive to maintain and fragile to change, reducing the velocity of both consumer and provider.

Using rigid exact-match assertions on response bodies: every provider-side field addition or formatting tweak breaks the contract, flooding the provider with irrelevant failures and incentivising looser matchers that defeat the purpose.

Creating one monolithic contract per consumer-provider pair: all interactions live in a single file, so adding one new interaction causes the entire contract to be re-verified and a conflict to emerge for all existing interactions simultaneously.

Circular consumer-provider dependency through contracts: service A contract depends on service B, and service B contract depends on service A - provider-side verification cannot run without a deployment order, and任何一个的失败都会级联放大.

Using the standard event-centric message pact workflow for command-pattern messaging (asymmetric request-response over a queue): Pact's provider-as-producer model fits events but not commands, leading to role-swap workarounds that confuse teams and drift from the intended CDC semantics.
design_principles: Robustness principle (Postel's law): be conservative in what the consumer requires and liberal in what it accepts - pin the requests, loosen the responses.
Loose coupling for independent deployability: constrain only what the consumer depends on, leaving unrelated provider change free.
YAGNI applied to integration: every interaction must earn its place by catching a real consumer-visible break.
Separation of concerns: contract verification (compatibility) is distinct from functional verification (correctness), and both are distinct from end-to-end assurance.
Shift left and the test pyramid: replace a slow shared-environment check with fast isolated tests in both repositories.
Explicit contracts over implicit assumptions: consumer expectations become an artifact that can be reviewed, versioned and diffed.
Contracts are immutable once published: a versioned contract represents a frozen agreement; any change from the consumer side produces a new contract version, never an in-place update.
Verification is a provider responsibility: the consumer writes the contract, but the provider is obligated to verify it and gate its own deployments on the result.
Small, focused interactions over large scenario contracts: each interaction should represent one request-response pair; multi-step scenarios belong in end-to-end tests, not in contracts.
best_practices: Write the consumer test against the client class that owns the HTTP or messaging interaction - not a raw generic client - and inject the mock URL through configuration.
Match exactly what the consumer sends and use matcher-based matching (type, regex, each-like, constrained array) for what it receives, decided field by field.
Assert only what would break the consumer if it changed; leave provider data and business rules the consumer never reads out of the contract.
Make provider states explicit and parameterized, and reset provider data per interaction so every interaction verifies in isolation.
Run verification on every provider build, publish the results, and gate deployment on the compatibility of the specific versions being released.
Treat contracts as build outputs: clean stale files so an interaction the consumer no longer sends cannot keep verifying.
Keep end-to-end tests for the journeys that need them and use the contract to generate stubs where the provider is not available.

Use the broker's can-i-deploy check in CI/CD pipelines to prevent incompatible versions from reaching production: query the broker for the matrix of consumer and provider versions before promoting a release.
Use pending (wip) contracts for new interactions under development: mark them as wip to prevent provider verification failures from blocking the build while the interface is still evolving.
Publish contracts as immutable artifacts keyed to a semantic consumer version: never overwrite a published contract - a changed consumer expectation is a new version.

Start with one contract per consumer-provider pair and split only when the verification matrix becomes dense; use tagging or labels to distinguish interaction categories before introducing separate contracts.
Keep provider state handlers lean: model only the data needed for the interaction to succeed, not the full application state; prefer factory methods over elaborate fixture scripts.

Use content matchers judiciously on the provider side: prefer type and format matchers for body fields, regex for structured strings, and each_value for collections; reserve exact matching for fields the consumer explicitly depends on.

Version contracts with the consumer: the contract version should track the consumer version that produced it, so the provider can read the compatibility matrix and understand which consumer versions are affected by a change.
Run consumer tests in CI before publishing the contract, to ensure the contract represents a green, passing test - never publish a contract from a failed or skipped test run.
Separate consumer contract tests from consumer unit tests: contract tests live close to the integration boundary and may require different fixture setup; keep them fast enough to run on every commit.

Document provider states with the same rigour as the contract itself: state names are part of the contract's API to the provider; drift between state names and state handler implementations is a common source of silent verification failures.

Use git commit SHA as the application version when publishing contracts and verification results: meaningful unique versions are what make can-i-deploy trustworthy and enable accurate deployment recording.

Wire broker webhooks into the provider CI pipeline so that when a consumer publishes a new pact (contract_content_changed event), the provider build is automatically triggered - removing manual coordination between teams.

For message and event contracts, separate message handling logic from transport layer concerns: test that the handler can process the message shape in isolation; Pact contracts the data, not how it travels (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ, SNS are all abstracted).

Apply the Robustness Principle field-by-field: consumer tests should use type matchers (like, stringType, numberType) for response data and reserve exact value matching only for values the consumer logic explicitly depends on - over-specification is the most common source of brittle contracts.

When testing commands (asymmetric request-response over a queue) rather than events (broadcast), consider swapping consumer/provider roles or using a hybrid approach since the standard message pact workflow is event-centric.

For Kafka with Schema Registry, use the schema-registry content type (application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json) so Pact augments messages with the 5 magic bytes and the consumer handler must be able to skip them during deserialization - ensuring real-world compatibility.

Use TestContainers or dockerized dependencies for provider state when integration-like realism is needed beyond what mocking provides, but prefer code-level mocks (dependency injection) for speed, isolation and edge-case coverage.

Record deployments in the broker after each successful deploy (pact-broker record-deployment): the broker's compatibility matrix is only as accurate as the deployment history recorded in it; unrecorded deployments create gaps in can-i-deploy results.

Enable provider-side self-verification of OpenAPI/spec schemas as a complementary guard even when using CDCT: tools like Schemathesis or Dredd can catch schema drift that contract tests alone may miss.

Use contract versioning to manage breaking changes: additive changes (new optional fields) are safe; removals and type changes require consumer migration; use the broker matrix to identify all affected consumer versions before proceeding.

For hybrid CDCT+BDCT migration, run both verification models in parallel during transition: the broker can hold both a CDCT verification result and a BDCT cross-contract comparison for the same pair, allowing incremental migration consumer-by-consumer.
pitfalls: The broker becomes a single point of failure: if the broker is down, contract publishing and verification results are unavailable, blocking both consumer and provider pipelines - treat the broker as a production-grade service with appropriate redundancy and uptime SLAs.

Too many consumers on one provider creates a de-facto compatibility matrix that resists any breaking change, even legitimate ones: use contract versioning and the can-i-deploy matrix to manage this proactively rather than letting it become a political obstacle.

Provider states drift from production reality: state handlers are maintained separately from the provider codebase and can develop their own bugs; review state handlers during provider code review and treat them as first-class citizens.

Loose matchers on the provider side create false positives: a contract passes verification but the real consumer response handling breaks because a semantic constraint (units, date formats, URL structure) was not captured.

Forgetting to publish verification results after a provider build: the broker has no record of the verification, so can-i-deploy queries return incomplete data and the deployment gate becomes unreliable.

Circular contract dependencies between services create a deployment order problem: service A's contract depends on service B and vice versa, making independent deployment impossible - resolve by extracting a shared domain event contract or by restructuring the interaction.

Over-specifying response contracts with exact values: every harmless data change (a timestamp, a dynamically generated ID, a localised string) breaks provider verification and trains teams to loosen matchers to the point of meaninglessness; use type and regex matchers aggressively for response data.

Skipping request validation in the consumer mock: if the mock accepts any request and returns the declared response without asserting what the client actually sent, the contract records nothing about the consumer's expectations and becomes a documentation artifact rather than a test artifact.

State string typos between consumer and provider: a consumer declares "order 123 exists" but the provider handler implements "Order 123 exists" - a silent mismatch that causes every verification to fail for data reasons unrelated to the API contract.

Publishing contracts from failed or skipped test runs: a contract that reflects a test that was disabled, parameterized to the wrong values, or that did not execute the real client code is worse than no contract - it provides false confidence.

Using CDCT to test business logic or data correctness: contract tests pin the shape of the wire format, not the meaning of the data; attempting to test provider business rules through a contract test makes the contract brittle and the provider's legitimate internal changes fail.

Not wiring can-i-deploy into the deployment pipeline: running contract verification but ignoring the result during promotions means contracts become informational rather than enforced; treat a failed can-i-deploy as a blocking build failure.

Forgetting to record deployments in the broker: without pact-broker record-deployment, the broker's matrix of "what is currently deployed" is based on assumption rather than fact, causing can-i-deploy to return false negatives (incorrectly approving incompatible combinations).

State handler proliferation: each interaction declaring an elaborate named state leads to a large catalog of state handlers that must all be maintained in sync with the provider's evolving data model; keep states lean and parameterized rather than one-per-scenario.

Ignoring backward compatibility in event-driven systems: old messages can be in-flight or replayed from an event store long after a provider version ships, so removing or renaming fields in event contracts can break consumers processing historical events; always treat message schemas as append-only or version the topic.

Treating BDCT as a replacement for CDCT without understanding the coverage gap: BDCT statically compares schemas and does not catch behavioral bugs (conditional responses, computed fields, state-dependent behaviour) that only emerge when the provider code is exercised end-to-end.

Wrong move: authoring or hand-maintaining the contract on the producer side (e.g. Spring Cloud Contract contracts written where only consumer tests change) -> the consumer's client code drifts from the contract - deleting a field from the client never invalidates the contract - so the provider keeps verifying an obsolete agreement and real breakage ships green -> instead derive the contract from code the consumer's test run actually executes, so an unexercised expectation cannot survive the build.

Wrong move: adopting contracts for one convenient consumer-provider pair while other consumers of the same provider opt out -> verification reports green across the adopting pair while the non-adopting consumer still breaks in production, and the team believes the boundary is protected -> instead roll the pattern out over one boundary's complete consumer set (or the provider's whole dependency graph) before trusting the gate, since partial adoption yields almost no safety for the same operational cost.

Wrong move: keeping both a provider-owned OpenAPI/schema and consumer-owned contract files as independent sources of truth -> the two artifacts drift apart, stubs generated from one disagree with verifications run against the other, and each incident spawns negotiation over which artifact was authoritative -> instead pick one authoritative artifact per boundary (or generate one from the other in CI) so a mismatch is a build failure, not an arbitration.
